Stated Claim / Post Context:
CVS to Pay $315M Over Dangerous Opioid Prescriptions

=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: CVS to Pay $315M Over Dangerous Opioid Prescriptions ===

[Source 1 — balleralert.com] (URL: https://balleralert.com/cvs-315-million-opioid-settlement-dangerous-prescriptions/?utm_source=dlvr.it&utm_medium=bluesky):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
CVS to Pay $315M Over Dangerous Opioid Prescriptions

CVS agrees to a $315 million settlement over allegations it filled illegal opioid prescriptions, ignored safety warnings, and put patients at risk.

Actual Article Body:
CVS Hit With $315 Million Settlement After Allegedly Filling Dangerous Opioid Prescriptions That Could Kill Patients

CVS Health is facing a $315 million settlement after federal investigators accused the pharmacy giant of dispensing dangerous amounts of prescription opioids, filling questionable prescriptions, and allowing business practices that allegedly put profits ahead of patients’ lives.

On Tuesday, October 13, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice announced that CVS Pharmacy and its related companies agreed to the massive payout to resolve allegations involving illegally dispensed opioids and other controlled substances.

The federal government claims the alleged misconduct occurred between October 17, 2013, and December 2, 2025, spanning more than 12 years.

According to investigators, CVS knowingly filled prescriptions that lacked legitimate medical purposes, including excessive quantities of opioids, prescriptions filled earlier than medically appropriate, and dangerous combinations of medications.

Some prescriptions allegedly originated from doctors operating so-called “pill mills,” where controlled substances were prescribed in large quantities without legitimate medical justification.

Even more concerning, federal officials allege CVS pharmacists continued dispensing certain prescriptions despite warning signs that the medications could be inappropriate or unlawful.

Among the most alarming allegations is that CVS dispensed prescriptions for a combination of three medications commonly referred to as the “trinity.”

The combination includes an opioid painkiller, a benzodiazepine, often prescribed for anxiety, and a muscle relaxant.

When taken together, these medications can dangerously suppress the central nervous system, potentially slowing or stopping a person’s breathing.

According to the Food and Drug Administration, combining opioids with benzodiazepines and other sedating medications increases the risk of extreme drowsiness, respiratory depression, coma, and death.

Federal investigators also accused CVS of dispensing excessive quantities of opioids and filling prescriptions too early.

These practices can increase the risk of misuse, dependence, addiction, and overdose, particularly when patients receive more medication than medically necessary.

Prescription opioids, including oxycodone and hydrocodone, can provide legitimate pain relief when appropriately prescribed. However, their potentially addictive properties and overdose risks make careful monitoring essential.

The government alleges CVS repeatedly overlooked warning signs that should have triggered additional scrutiny.

Beyond the prescriptions themselves, federal prosecutors raised concerns about CVS’s internal operations.

The government’s complaint alleges the company maintained performance metrics, employee incentives, and staffing policies that prioritized financial results over patient protection.

Investigators claimed CVS failed to provide adequate pharmacist staffing while simultaneously expecting employees to meet corporate performance targets.

Federal officials also alleged certain company policies prevented pharmacists from warning their colleagues about suspicious prescribers.

Those alleged restrictions could have made identifying dangerous prescribing patterns more difficult.

The investigation further found allegations that CVS submitted claims for reimbursement to Medicare and other federally funded healthcare programs for prescriptions that investigators considered invalid.

Consequently, the allegations involve potential violations of both the Controlled Substances Act and the False Claims Act.

The Justice Department emphasized that pharmacies have a responsibility to verify questionable prescriptions rather than simply dispensing medication.

Under the agreement, CVS must implement stronger monitoring procedures intended to identify suspicious prescriptions and potentially dangerous dispensing patterns.

The company has entered into an agreement with the Drug Enforcement Administration requiring it to monitor pharmacy dispensing practices, establish procedures for reviewing questionable prescribers, and create a hotline where employees and members of the public can report suspected unlawful dispensing.

Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate explained the significance of the new requirements.

“Today’s settlement requires CVS to implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate,” he stated.

“The remedial measures in this agreement — including proactive monitoring of opioid prescribing patterns — will provide critical protections for patients and federal healthcare programs. The Department of Justice will continue to take steps to prevent the unlawful dispensing of opioids.”

Despite agreeing to the settlement, CVS maintains that it did not violate federal law.

“Our more than 27,000 CVS pharmacists do their part to help keep America healthy and are highly trained in the safe and appropriate use of all medications. We’ve implemented best-in-class and first-of-their-kind programs to help our pharmacists make the best decisions on behalf of patients,” CVS Health said in a statement Tuesday.

The company further rejected the government’s characterization of its dispensing practices.

“We strongly disagree with the claims made in this case, and our settlement with the DOJ admits no wrongdoing. We’re pleased to move forward and put this litigation behind us,” the company added.

The agreement does not constitute an admission of liability, and a court has not determined that CVS committed the alleged violations.

The litigation originated with allegations brought by former CVS employee Hillary Estright under federal whistleblower protections.

This latest agreement adds to CVS’s previous multibillion-dollar opioid settlements.

In 2022, the pharmacy giant agreed to pay approximately $4.9 billion to state and local governments and other eligible jurisdictions to resolve thousands of opioid-related claims.

Other major pharmacy retailers, including Walgreens, Kroger, and Walmart, have also faced settlements connected to prescription opioid dispensing.

The broader public health stakes remain significant.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately 44,564 Americans died from opioid-involved overdoses in 2025, based on provisional estimates. Although that represents a decline from 2024, opioid-related deaths remain a serious national concern.

The statistics do not establish that CVS’s alleged dispensing practices caused any particular overdose death.

Still, the settlement underscores the importance of pharmacy oversight, especially when medications carry substantial risks of addiction and fatal overdose.

For CVS, the $315 million payout closes a major legal dispute without an admission of wrongdoing. For federal regulators, the agreement represents another effort to ensure that warning signs surrounding dangerous prescriptions are no longer overlooked.

Actual Article Body:

TOK PISIN

By Callum Liddelow

Topic:Police

The man's speed camera car, similar to this one, was impounded after the alleged offence. (Supplied, file photo)

A speed camera operator has been charged with reckless driving after he allegedly used his work car to perform a dangerous overtaking manoeuvre in WA's Wheatbelt region, causing an oncoming vehicle to swerve off the road.

Police say the 67-year-old Toodyay man was driving a white Isuzu D-Max utility along Great Eastern Highway around 12pm on Tuesday, September 29, while working near the towns of Tammin and Cunderdin, about 145 kilometres east of Perth.

It is alleged he overtook a road train in a "dangerous and unsafe" manner, forcing an oncoming car to brake and turn onto the shoulder of the road to avoid a head-on collision.

Police have charged the Road Safety Commission employee after an investigation. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

Police say they began conducting "extensive inquiries", collecting video footage and interviewing drivers involved in the incident.

As a result of that investigation, the Road Safety Commission (RSC) employee was charged with reckless driving, and his speed camera car was impounded.

The vehicle was released on October 12 after a request from the RSC, and the man's personal vehicle was impounded in its place.

Do you know more? Contact Callum Liddelow.

The man is expected to face Northam Magistrates Court on December 14.

In a statement, WA Police reminded drivers to remain patient and exercise caution when overtaking heavy vehicles.

The RSC has been contacted for comment.
